title: AI Is Changing How Freelance Work Comes Together
summary: New research from Upwork and OpenAI finds AI-related freelance projects pair familiar tasks in less common ways, offering an early look at how work is changing.
body_markdown:
### New Upwork–OpenAI research finds freelance AI projects combine familiar work in new ways.


By Teng Liu


### **Key Insights**


In a[report with OpenAI’s Economic Research team](https://openai.com/index/ai-effect-on-freelance-work/) , we compare how people use ChatGPT for work with the projects clients post on Upwork Marketplace. People use ChatGPT more often for writing and advice, while businesses post on Upwork more often for technical implementation and finished deliverables. AI-related projects are also associated with larger budgets and more hours of work. And in AI-related projects, combinations of tasks that were rarely seen together before generative AI are more than three times as common as in other projects. Think AI-generated video paired with motion graphics, or chatbot development with app integration. Businesses are asking for work that spans AI-related and established tasks—an early signal that roles may be changing from within. Freelancers and workers who can anticipate these shifts and shape the mix of tasks they take on may be better positioned to pursue emerging opportunities. As AI tools and freelance marketplaces integrate, future research should examine which combinations of AI and human expertise deliver the best results.


## **How jobs may change from within**


AI may change the work people do before it changes job titles or formal[job descriptions](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35987) . Jobs are, in practice, bundles of tasks. A marketer, designer, analyst, or software developer is defined not only by a title, but by the mix of tasks they are expected to perform and the outcomes they are accountable for delivering.


That mix can change before an occupation visibly changes. An occupation such as software engineering is unlikely to change all at once. Some activities may be automated or supported by AI, while others remain human-led or shift toward review, integration, and coordination. A company may keep the same job title and headcount while reallocating parts of the work to AI, or asking one person to coordinate capabilities that were previously spread across several specialists. Two people with the same title may therefore see very different changes in their day-to-day work.


One way to see how AI is showing up in work is to compare what people ask ChatGPT to help with and what businesses seek from freelancers. In sampled ChatGPT conversations, writing and advice feature prominently; Upwork postings more often seek technical implementation, visual production, and finished deliverables. Because the datasets aren’t linked person to person, we can’t trace a path from ChatGPT use to a freelance hire. The comparison does show different mixes of work across the two settings. We next examine how tasks come together within AI-related Upwork projects.


## **AI-related projects pair familiar tasks in unfamiliar ways**


To check how AI-related work differs from other freelance work, we analyze Upwork Marketplace job posts through 2025. We classify a posting as AI-related when it requests AI skills or tools, or involves improving AI-generated output. Each posting can contain multiple tasks, allowing us to examine not only which tasks clients request, but which tasks they request together.


The first finding is that AI-related projects more often combine tasks that had rarely appeared together before. As shown in Figure 1, 8% of task pairs in AI-related job posts were historically uncommon, compared with 2% in non-AI posts. A task pair is two tasks requested in the same post, and “historically uncommon” means the pair showed up in very few postings before the generative AI era (late 2022). More than half of these uncommon pairs join an AI-related task with a traditional one. The tasks themselves are not new; it’s the pairings that are. For example:


- AI-generated video with motion graphics
- AI integration with campaign management
- Chatbot development with app integration


**Figure 1: AI-related projects are more than three times as likely to pair tasks in historically uncommon ways**


*Source: Upwork Marketplace data*


This is not simply because AI-related projects may contain more tasks in general. They average only slightly more tasks per posting than other projects—3.35, compared with 3.19. The more notable difference is in the combination itself. Consider a business building an AI-powered lead-generation workflow. The project may combine AI integration, customer-data organization, marketing automation, and campaign management. The value lies not in any one component, but in connecting them into a system that can support a business outcome.


This pattern holds across project sizes, even when comparing similar types of work and timeframe, as shown in Figure 2.


**Figure 2: AI-related projects show more novel task combinations across project sizes**


*Source: Upwork Marketplace data*


Together, these findings suggest that AI-related projects are not simply adding tasks to familiar work. They more often combine tasks in ways that were rare before.


The difference also appears in project scope. After accounting for work category and posting month, budgets listed for AI-related fixed-price projects were 52% higher than for non-AI projects. Among hourly contracts that were hired and had recorded hours, freelancers worked 41% more hours in their first 90 days. Posted hourly rates were about 1.5% higher. These comparisons suggest greater project scope and more hours worked, alongside a modest difference in posted hourly rates.


Freelance marketplace data cannot necessarily establish that the same changes are already occurring inside firms. But because clients can revise a project description quickly, it can provide an early view of the new combinations of work that businesses are beginning to demand. That matters because, even amid substantial disruption, AI’s effects may be absorbed partly through adjustment within occupations rather than wholesale occupational displacement. Recent[McKinsey Global Institute projections](https://www.mckinsey.com/mgi/our-research/workforce-in-motion-skills-and-pathways-to-future-jobs-in-the-united-states) similarly suggest that many workers may remain in their current occupations as the tasks, skills, and workflows within those roles change. The task recombination we observe here may be one early example of how that adjustment begins.


An important next step is to move beyond identifying new task combinations to understanding how people and AI collaborate to deliver outcomes: when does AI help someone complete a project independently, and when does human expertise become essential? This study cannot trace that process, but connecting AI tools with freelance marketplaces could create opportunities to examine how work moves between people and AI—and which combinations lead to better results.


Upwork’s Model Context Protocol ([MCP](https://investors.upwork.com/news-releases/news-release-details/upwork-talent-now-everywhere-ai-works) ) server brings its marketplace into AI tools such as[ChatGPT](https://www.upwork.com/ai/plugins) , helping businesses access human expertise within the work already underway. Looking ahead, these connections could enable AI agents to engage experts autonomously within user-defined budgets, permissions, and criteria—for example, to verify an output or resolve a task requiring human judgment. Studying these workflows could deepen our understanding of how human expertise and AI capabilities come together to turn intent into completed work.


## **Methodology**


The research report mainly uses a sample of Upwork Marketplace job posts through 2025. These job posts are represented using more than 3,000 detailed activity descriptions, which are grouped into more than 400 standardized task clusters of closely related work. We classify postings as AI-related when they request AI skills or tools, or involve improving AI-generated output. For Figure 1, we identify every distinct pair of task clusters within each posting and calculate the share that had appeared together in fewer than 200 pre-generative-AI postings, including pairs with no prior observed occurrence; we then average that share across AI-related and non-AI-related jobs. Figure 2 reports coefficients from separate ordinary least squares regressions comparing the historical rarity of task pairs in AI-related and non-AI-related jobs. The outcome is each job’s average task-pair novelty score, based on the pre-generative-AI prevalence of pairs observed at least 20 times in the reference period; the models account for project bundle size, work subcategory, and posting month. These results describe patterns in this sample and do not necessarily imply AI causal impact. Full data, classification, and modeling details are available in the accompanying report.

## **About the author**


Dr. Teng Liu is an economist at Upwork, where he studies how AI and technological change are transforming the labor market and reshaping skill demand. He holds a Ph.D. in economics from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and specializes in labor market dynamics and quantitative research. His work informs Upwork’s insights on workforce shifts, economic opportunity, and policy.
